benchmark: Cārvāka-standard continuous master with a topic-specific Political Theory twelve-panel atlas

topics.title: Power, Authority and Legitimacy
topics.benchmark_preservation: The approved design reference, prior topic artifacts and canonical Political Theory owners remain immutable.

lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Power, Authority, Legitimacy and Influence
[1] Power secures effects; authority is power accepted as rightful.
v
[2] Legitimacy explains willing compliance while influence works without direct force.
v
[3] Gauba's formula authority equals power plus legitimacy anchors the topic.
v
[4] Consent must still be tested for manipulation, exclusion and unequal resources.
v
VERDICT -> Authority adds accepted rightfulness to the capacity called power.
ANSWER USE -> Define all four adjacent concepts before comparing them.

panels.panel_title: Power Forms, Core Distinctions and Chapter Spine
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Power Forms, Core Distinctions and Chapter Spine
[1] Political, economic and ideological power operate through different resources.
v
[2] Coercion threatens sanctions; hegemony organises consent in civil society.
v
[3] Power over identifies domination; power to identifies capacity and resistance.
v
[4] A complete answer asks who rules, by what means and with what acceptance.
v
VERDICT -> Power travels through resources, coercion, belief and capacity.
ANSWER USE -> State the mechanism and location rather than only naming a thinker.

panels.panel_title: Weber, Marx, Gramsci and Classical Elite Theory
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Weber, Marx, Gramsci and Classical Elite Theory
[1] Weber classifies traditional, charismatic and legal-rational authority.
v
[2] Marx and Engels locate political power in class ownership and production.
v
[3] Gramsci adds hegemony, civil society and relative autonomy.
v
[4] Pareto, Mosca, Michels and Mills analyse different forms of minority rule.
v
VERDICT -> Authority, class, hegemony and elite organisation locate power differently.
ANSWER USE -> Attach every thinker to one mechanism and one limitation.

panels.panel_title: Pluralism, Deep Power, Feminism and Constructive Power
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Pluralism, Deep Power, Feminism and Constructive Power
[1] Pareto and Mosca explain circulation among ruling minorities.
v
[2] Michels explains the organisational tendency toward oligarchic leadership.
v
[3] Elite turnover can coexist with oligarchy; the claims are not strict opposites.
v
[4] Pluralism, Lukes, feminism, Arendt and Macpherson widen the power map.
v
VERDICT -> Elite circulation and organisational oligarchy can coexist.
ANSWER USE -> Compare personnel turnover with control of organisational machinery.

panels.panel_title: Comparisons, Traps, Boundaries and Source Discipline
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Comparisons, Traps, Boundaries and Source Discipline
[1] Visible decisions form the first dimension of power.
v
[2] Agenda exclusion forms the second; preference shaping forms the third.
v
[3] The third dimension is a contested hypothesis, not a proven finding.
v
[4] Arendt and Macpherson restore collective and developmental power to the analysis.
v
VERDICT -> Each dimension deepens power analysis but raises a harder evidence burden.
ANSWER USE -> Treat preference shaping as a contestable hypothesis, not a finding.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Theses, Directives and Perspective Selection
[1] A thesis must distinguish capacity, rightfulness and willing compliance.
v
[2] Directive control decides whether one perspective or several must be compared.
v
[3] Elite answers separate circulation of personnel from organisation-level oligarchy.
v
[4] Digital answers distinguish public, private and hybrid power.
v
VERDICT -> Directive control prevents power theories from becoming an unranked list.
ANSWER USE -> Select dimensions and perspectives that answer the exact demand.

panels.panel_title: Elite-Theory Debate, Evidence and Mark Scaling
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Elite-Theory Debate, Evidence and Mark Scaling
[1] Authority is more stable than force because legitimacy lowers coercive costs.
v
[2] Lukes replies that apparent consent may itself be shaped by deeper power.
v
[3] The objection is difficult to verify without observable mechanisms.
v
[4] Use defaults, exclusions and barriers to contestation before claiming false
interests.
v
VERDICT -> Consent may legitimate authority or reveal hegemony and hidden domination.
ANSWER USE -> Test acceptance through contestability, resources and alternatives.

panels.panel_title: Digital Power: Panopticism, Data and the Three Dimensions
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Digital Power: Panopticism, Data and the Three Dimensions
[1] Panopticism explains self-policing under uncertain observation.
v
[2] Data power adds asymmetric knowledge, ranking, prediction and automated discretion.
v
[3] Foucault, Zuboff and Pariser are extensions beyond Gauba and remain paraphrased.
v
[4] The M.A.N.A.V. vision supplies a current ethical-governance anchor.
v
VERDICT -> Digital power extends classical mechanisms without erasing provenance limits.
ANSWER USE -> Mark Foucault, Zuboff and Pariser as later conceptual extensions.

panels.panel_title: Surveillance Asymmetry, Consent and the Public-Private Boundary
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Surveillance Asymmetry, Consent and the Public-Private Boundary
[1] Surveillance can chill association, hide criteria and aggregate minor observations.
v
[2] Formal consent may be thin when terms are unread and participation is necessary.
v
[3] Platform power strains public accountability and ordinary market exit.
v
[4] Legitimate power requires explanation, review and meaningful answerability.
v
VERDICT -> Private and hybrid power expose an accountability gap beyond state coercion.
ANSWER USE -> Ask who decides, who can challenge and whether exit is meaningful.

panels.panel_title: Objections, Puttaswamy Boundary and Digital Answer Architecture
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Objections, Puttaswamy Boundary and Digital Answer Architecture
[1] Puttaswamy is used only as a structured-justification conceptual anchor.
v
[2] No statutory, programme or current regulatory detail is authored here.
v
[3] Three objections test voluntariness, unfalsifiability and state-centrism.
v
[4] A graded verdict separates technological capacity from rightful authority.
v
VERDICT -> Structured justification, not technological novelty, is the legitimacy test.
ANSWER USE -> Conclude with legality, proportionality, explanation and review.
CENTRAL FOCUS
MCQ Remediation and Trap Repair
[1] Close options test power versus authority and coercion versus hegemony.
v
[2] They separate Weber's types, elite mechanisms and the three power dimensions.
v
[3] Michels does not prove permanent, unchanging oligarchy in every organisation.
v
[4] Third-dimensional preference shaping must not be asserted as an established fact.
v
VERDICT -> Close options turn on mechanism, depth, location and source boundary.
ANSWER USE -> Reject overclaims about permanent oligarchy or manufactured preferences.
CENTRAL FOCUS
PYQ Ownership and Answer Practice
[1] No directly owned verified UPSC PYQ is assigned to this topic.
v
[2] Six original questions test concepts, elite theory, pluralism and digital power.
v
[3] A strong answer adds Arendt or Macpherson as a constructive counterpoint.
v
[4] Final recall: capacity becomes authority only through legitimate answerability.
v
VERDICT -> Original practice integrates classical power with its digital extension.
ANSWER USE -> End by separating bare capacity from legitimate and answerable authority.
